323.title: The ones who carry it
323.hook: millions have memorized the whole Qur'an, many as children
323.howItsDone: Many Muslim children and adults memorize the Qur'an in dedicated schools and circles, reciting a new portion to a teacher each day and revising what they know; a hafiz often leads the long Ramadan night prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, qira'at: the readings, passed down in chains of reciters. Your line was many voices, one text. What did you hear that was the same underneath? Day three hundred twenty-three.

In a small room in Cairo, or Kano, or Karachi, or a converted storefront in Minneapolis, a boy of eleven stands in front of his teacher and a row of family. Over the next hours, he recites. Not a surah. The whole Qur'an, from al-Fatiha to An-Nas, from memory, while the teacher follows along and listens for a single slip. When he finishes, his mother is crying. There's a word for what he has become. Today: the ones who carry it.
screen: `A BOY OF ELEVEN STANDS UP.` → `THE WHOLE QUR'AN, FROM MEMORY.` → `HIS MOTHER IS CRYING.`

segments.voice: The word is hafiz, and for a woman, hafizah. It comes from a root meaning to guard, to preserve, to keep. You've heard that root in the Qur'an itself. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! We, even We, reveal the Reminder, and lo! We verily are its Guardian." Guardian there comes from the same root. Muslims see the memorizers as part of how that guarding happens: the book is kept not only on paper but in people. Nobody has an exact count, but many millions of Muslims alive today are thought to have memorized the whole Qur'an, and far more carry large parts of it. Many begin as children, in schools built for exactly this, going over a few lines at a time, reciting each day's new portion to a teacher and revising the old. The Qur'an seems made for it. Its rhythm and rhyme hold together in the memory. And it says of itself, in Pickthall: "And in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; but is there any that remembereth?" The Prophet ﷺ spoke about those who carry it. A hadith says the one who recites the Qur'an skillfully will be with the noble, righteous scribes, the angels; and the one who recites it with difficulty, stumbling over it, gets a double reward. Stumbling, and still going, counts twice. The title even reached poetry: the Persian poet Hafez of Shiraz took his name because he knew the Qur'an by heart. And it isn't finished when the last surah is learned. Ask any hafiz: the hard part is keeping it. The Prophet compared it to a hobbled camel. Tend it, or it slips away.
screen: `HAFIZ: ONE WHO GUARDS AND KEEPS` · `MILLIONS, MANY AS CHILDREN` · `STUMBLING COUNTS TWICE` · `TEND IT, LIKE A HOBBLED CAMEL`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one new verse by heart. Choose one short verse you don't know yet. The second line of al-Ikhlas is a gentle place to start: Allahus-samad. Or any line you love. Say it five times, slowly, looking at it. Then five times with your eyes closed. Stumble if you stumble: it counts. If you're here to learn about the path rather than to practice it, learn the verse's meaning by heart instead. The bell holds the time.
Hafiz. One who has memorized the whole Qur'an: literally a guardian, a keeper. For a woman, hafizah. Today's word.
Your line: carried by heart. Today, say your new verse three times at odd moments, in line at a store, on the stairs, before a meal, so it starts to live in you. Day three hundred twenty-three.

324.title: Prostration verses
324.hook: places marked in the mushaf where the reciter prostrates
324.howItsDone: When Muslims recite or hear one of the marked prostration verses, many make a single prostration on the spot, in prayer or outside it, and the whole congregation follows the imam when he does.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hafiz: the ones who keep the whole Qur'an by heart. Your line was carried by heart. Did your new verse come back to you at an odd moment? Day three hundred twenty-four.

Imagine you're in a mosque, listening to the imam recite. Suddenly, in the middle of a surah, without a word of warning, he goes down: forehead to the floor. And the whole room goes with him. A few seconds later everyone rises, and the recitation carries on as if nothing happened. If you didn't know, you'd be left wondering what you'd missed. You missed a verse that bows. Today: prostration verses.
screen: `MID-SURAH, HE GOES DOWN.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM GOES WITH HIM.` → `A VERSE THAT BOWS.`

segments.voice: Scattered through the Qur'an are places where the text itself speaks of bowing down: the angels, the stars and the trees, the prophets, the believers who fall down in prostration when the verses are recited to them. At such places the Prophet ﷺ would prostrate when he recited or heard them. It's called the prostration of recitation, and the verses are called sajdah verses. Sajdah means a single prostration, from the same root as masjid, a mosque: the place of prostration. How many are there? Fourteen or fifteen, depending on the school of law. The schools also differ on whether it's required. Most scholars hold it's a strongly encouraged sunnah; the Hanafi school holds it obligatory for the one who recites or hears it. In a printed mushaf the places are marked, often with a line over the key word and a sign in the margin. There's a story in Bukhari: once the Prophet recited Surah an-Najm, and at its end he prostrated, and everyone with him prostrated too. And a hadith in Muslim says that when a person prostrates at such a verse, Satan withdraws, weeping, because he was commanded to bow and refused. The last sajdah in the book comes at the close of Surah al-'Alaq, the surah of the first revelation. In Pickthall's words: "Nay! Obey not thou him. But prostrate thyself, and draw near (unto Allah)." Prostrate, and draw near. That's the idea in one line: the lowest point of the body is the nearest point to God. There's even a surah named for it: Surah 32, as-Sajdah.
screen: `VERSES THAT SPEAK OF BOWING` · `FOURTEEN OR FIFTEEN PLACES` · `MARKED IN THE MARGIN` · `PROSTRATE, AND DRAW NEAR`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one prostration verse. After the bell, open a mushaf and look for the mark in the margin; the last verse of al-'Alaq is the easiest to find. For now, if you pray, you can make one prostration, forehead to the floor, and stay there for a few breaths. If you don't, simply lower your head, or rest your forehead on your hands, and notice how it feels to put the highest part of you at the lowest point. The bell holds the time.
Sajdah. A prostration, and the verses of the Qur'an where the reciter goes down to the ground. Today's word.

Your line: bow where it bows. Today, when something is bigger than you, a view, a kindness, a loss, let yourself be small in front of it for a moment instead of pushing back. Day three hundred twenty-four.

325.title: The longest and the shortest
325.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite al-Baqarah at home, in portions or in full, because of the hadith about the house where it is recited, and al-Kawthar is among the short surahs often recited in the daily prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sajdah: the verses where the reciter goes down to the ground. Your line was bow where it bows. Did you let yourself be small in front of something bigger? Day three hundred twenty-five.

Two surahs. One is so long that reciting it aloud takes well over an hour, and it fills nearly fifty pages of a standard mushaf. The other you can say in the time it takes to tie your shoes, and a child can learn it in an afternoon. They sit near opposite ends of the book, and Muslims hold that both are equally the word of God. Today: the longest and the shortest.
screen: `WELL OVER AN HOUR.` → `THE TIME IT TAKES TO TIE YOUR SHOES.` → `BOTH EQUALLY THE QUR'AN.`

segments.voice: The longest is al-Baqarah, the Cow, Surah 2, with two hundred and eighty-six verses. It's named for a story inside it: Musa telling his people to sacrifice a cow, and their endless questions stalling the command. Al-Baqarah holds almost everything: the story of Adam, the turning of the prayer toward Mecca, fasting in Ramadan, pilgrimage, charity, marriage and divorce, debts. It holds the longest single verse in the Qur'an, about writing down a loan, and Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse. And near its end, in Pickthall's words: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." The Prophet ﷺ said, in a hadith in Muslim: don't make your houses into graveyards; Satan flees from a house in which Surah al-Baqarah is recited. The shortest is al-Kawthar, Surah 108: three verses, about ten Arabic words. You learned it in camp four. "Lo! We have given thee Abundance;" then: so pray to your Lord, and sacrifice. Then: the one who hates you is the one cut off. Reports say it came at a hard time, when the Prophet's sons had died young and an enemy mocked him as cut off, a man with no line. Three verses to answer a grief. Here's what's worth noticing. A surah's weight isn't its length. Al-Kawthar is complete, a whole surah, just as al-Baqarah is. The Qur'an's challenge to bring a surah like it applies to the short ones as much as the long. And both open with the same bismillah. Long and short: some days you need the whole house, and some days one room is enough.
screen: `AL-BAQARAH: 286 VERSES` · `A HOUSE WHERE IT'S RECITED` · `AL-KAWTHAR: THREE VERSES` · `WEIGHT ISN'T LENGTH`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read al-Kawthar once more. If you know it, say it now, slowly, all three verses, bismillah first. If you don't, remember it in English: abundance; pray and sacrifice; the one cut off. Then sit with the first verse only. Abundance. What have you been given that you forget to count? Let one thing come to mind, and stay with it. If another comes, let it join the first. The bell holds the time.
The longest and the shortest. Al-Baqarah, two hundred and eighty-six verses; al-Kawthar, three. Each one a whole surah. Today's word.
screen: `THE LONGEST AND THE SHORTEST — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: long and short. Today, give one thing the long version, a real conversation, a slow meal, and let another be short and complete: a three-word thank you. Day three hundred twenty-five.

326.title: Who is speaking
326.hook: Allah speaks as I, We and He, and the shifts carry meaning
326.howItsDone: Students of the Qur'an learn to notice its shifts of voice, from We to I to He and the command 'say', and teachers often point to the turn in al-Fatiha as the first example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the longest and the shortest: al-Baqarah's two hundred eighty-six verses, al-Kawthar's three. Your line was long and short. What got the long version today? Day three hundred twenty-six.

Read al-Fatiha slowly, the way it is said in every prayer, and something happens in the middle. It begins by talking about God: praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, the Beneficent, the Merciful, Owner of the Day of Judgment. He, and He, and He. And then, suddenly, with no warning at all: Thee alone we worship. The one reciting turns from talking about God to talking to God. Today: who is speaking.
screen: `HE, AND HE, AND HE.` → `THEN, SUDDENLY: THEE.` → `WHO IS SPEAKING?`

segments.voice: That sudden turn has a name in Arabic rhetoric: iltifat, a turning, a shift of person. The Qur'an does it again and again, and it's one of the things that makes it feel alive, even startling, the first time you notice. In Pickthall's rendering of the Fatiha, the turn is plain: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help." Scholars say it's as if, after praising, the one praying has come near enough to speak face to face. Across the Qur'an, God speaks in more than one way. Very often as We: We sent down, We created. In Arabic this is the plural of majesty, the way a sovereign speaks, and Muslims understand it as grandeur, never as more than one God. The Qur'an is fierce about that oneness: Say, He is Allah, the One. God also speaks as I, and those moments are often the most intimate. In Pickthall's words: "And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh." Not We: I. Close. And God is spoken of as He, in the third person, as in much of the Fatiha. Then there's another voice: the Prophet ﷺ being told what to say. That's the small word qul, say, at the start of al-Ikhlas and the last surahs you learned. The Prophet isn't the author; he's being handed the words. Scholars treat these shifts as meaningful: We for power and creation, I for nearness and mercy, He for praise and description, say for the words passed on. Not every turn has an agreed explanation. But listening for who is speaking, and to whom, changes how a verse lands.
screen: `THE TURN IN THE FATIHA` · `WE: THE PLURAL OF MAJESTY` · `I: THE MOST INTIMATE` · `QUL: THE PROPHET IS TOLD TO SAY`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the voice in one verse. Take al-Ikhlas: say, He is Allah, the One. Ask three questions, slowly. Who is speaking? God, telling the Prophet. To whom? To the Prophet, and through him to everyone. About whom? About God, as He. Then try the Fatiha's turn: say the praise, pause, and say Thee alone we worship, and notice where your attention turns. The bell holds the time.
Who is speaking. The Qur'an's shifts of voice, We, I, He and say, and the meaning each one carries. Today's word.

Your line: listen for who is speaking. Today, in one conversation, notice when someone shifts from talking about a thing to talking to you. Something usually changes right there. Day three hundred twenty-six.

327.title: Handling the mushaf
327.hook: many keep it high, clean, and touch it only in wudu
327.howItsDone: Many Muslims make wudu before touching the Arabic mushaf, keep it on a high, clean shelf with nothing on top, read it on a stand, and bury or respectfully dispose of worn-out copies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, who is speaking: We, I, He, and say. Your line was listen for who is speaking. Did you catch a moment when someone turned to talk to you? Day three hundred twenty-seven.

Walk into many Muslim homes and look for the Qur'an. You probably won't find it on the floor, or under a pile of magazines, or on the bottom shelf beside the shoes. It'll be up high, often wrapped in cloth, sometimes on a shelf by itself. A grandmother may kiss it before she opens it. A child may be told never to put anything on top of it. Today: handling the mushaf.
screen: `NOT ON THE FLOOR.` → `UP HIGH, WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `NOTHING ON TOP OF IT.`

segments.voice: These customs come from how Muslims regard the Qur'an: the speech of God, written down. The written copy, the mushaf, is treated with the honor due to what it carries. The best-known rule is about touching it. Surah 56 describes the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words, as a book "Which none toucheth save the purified." Scholars read that verse in more than one way. Many understand it to be about the preserved book in heaven, touched only by angels. But most scholars of the four Sunni schools still hold that a person should be in a state of purity, with wudu, to touch the Arabic mushaf. They point also to a letter the Prophet ﷺ sent to Yemen, recorded in the Muwatta of Imam Malik: none should touch the Qur'an except one who is pure. Some scholars held otherwise, and there are discussions about children who are learning, about translations, and about phones and apps, which many say aren't a mushaf in the same sense. Beyond the rules there's a whole culture of care. A folding wooden stand holds it open so it doesn't lie on the floor. Many keep it on the highest shelf, with nothing placed on top. Many won't take it into a bathroom. When a copy wears out, it isn't thrown in the trash: it's buried, or respectfully burned, or placed in special boxes that some mosques keep. Some Muslims kiss it; others say no such practice is required, and simply handle it with care. What the customs share is simple. This isn't an ordinary book, so it doesn't get an ordinary place.
screen: `NONE TOUCHETH SAVE THE PURIFIED` · `MOST SCHOOLS: TOUCH IT WITH WUDU` · `A STAND, A HIGH SHELF, NOTHING ON TOP` · `WORN COPIES ARE BURIED, NOT TRASHED`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give your copy a clean shelf. If there's a mushaf or a translation in your home, after the bell, find it a clean, high place with nothing stacked on it. For now, sit and picture where it is right now. If you don't have one, think of the one book or object in your home you treat most carefully, and why. Notice what it feels like to honor something. If you pray, you might make wudu before you next open it. The bell holds the time.
Handling the mushaf. The care Muslims give a copy of the Qur'an: purity to touch it, a high place, and never the trash. Today's word.
Your line: keep it high. Today, move one thing you value off the floor or out from under a pile, and give it a place that says it matters. Day three hundred twenty-seven.

328.title: Khatm: the whole book
328.hook: finishing a whole reading, often in Ramadan, with a gathering
328.howItsDone: Many Muslims complete a full reading of the Qur'an in Ramadan, at home or through the tarawih prayers, and mosques and families often mark a khatm with a gathering, a special supplication and food.

segments.voice: Yesterday, handling the mushaf: purity to touch it, a high place, never the trash. Your line was keep it high. What did you give a better place? Day three hundred twenty-eight.

It's late on one of the last nights of Ramadan. The mosque is fuller than it's been all month. Children are awake long past their bedtimes. The imam is reciting An-Nas, the very last surah, and in many mosques, when he finishes, he goes straight back to the beginning and recites the opening of the book again. Then comes a long supplication. Some people are weeping; others are already handing out sweets. The whole book, finished. Today: khatm.
screen: `A LATE NIGHT IN RAMADAN.` → `THE LAST SURAH, THEN THE FIRST.` → `WEEPING, AND SWEETS.`

segments.voice: Khatm means a seal, a finishing. It's the same root as khatam, the seal, in the title Muslims give the Prophet ﷺ: the seal of the prophets. For the Qur'an, a khatm is one complete reading, from al-Fatiha to An-Nas. Ramadan is its season. The hadith collections say the angel Jibril went over the whole Qur'an with the Prophet every Ramadan, and twice in the year he died. So many Muslims try to finish at least one full reading during the month, alone at home, or by hearing it across the nights of tarawih, one juz' a night. When a mosque reaches the end, it's often a gathering, with a special supplication after the last surah, the du'a of khatm, often long and often tearful. There's a report that the companion Anas ibn Malik, when he finished the Qur'an, would gather his family and make du'a with them. Customs vary widely. In some places a child's first khatm is celebrated with a party and new clothes: in parts of South Asia it's called an Ameen, in Turkey a hatim. And in many places the reader who finishes An-Nas begins again at once from al-Fatiha, so the reading never really stops. How often? You met one hadith in the week of the thirty parts: once a month, and not faster than seven days. Another says the one who finishes in less than three days hasn't understood it. So speed isn't the point. Many people take a year, or several. A page a day finishes a standard mushaf in under two years. The point is the whole: not only the parts you love, but every page, once.
screen: `KHATM: A SEAL, A FINISHING` · `RAMADAN IS ITS SEASON` · `A GATHERING, A SUPPLICATION` · `BEGIN AGAIN FROM AL-FATIHA`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan next year's reading. Sit, and ask what's true for you. A juz' a day, a page a day, a few verses a day, or listening to one reciter through the whole book. There are about six hundred pages in a standard mushaf. Pick an amount you could keep on a bad day, not only a good one. If you're here to learn about the path rather than practice it, choose a translation of the meanings and a pace. Hold the plan quietly. The bell holds the time.
Khatm. A seal: one complete reading of the Qur'an, from al-Fatiha to An-Nas, often finished in Ramadan. Today's word.
Your line: the whole book, once. Today, write your plan somewhere you'll see it: how much, when in the day, and the date you hope to finish. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

329.title: Heard in the world
329.hook: from Jakarta to Dakar, the same Arabic is recited every day
329.howItsDone: Muslims everywhere recite the Qur'an in Arabic in their daily prayers, whatever language they speak at home, and each region has its own much-loved reciters and styles of recitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, khatm: the whole book, sealed, and begun again. Your line was the whole book, once. Did you write your plan down? Day three hundred twenty-nine, the end of a week.

Dawn is a moving line. Right now it's reaching a new strip of the earth, and somewhere in that strip, someone is standing to pray and reciting al-Fatiha. An hour from now the line will have moved west, and someone else will be saying the same seven verses in the same Arabic. Follow the dawn around the planet and you'll hear the Qur'an recited in every time zone. Today: heard in the world.

segments.voice: There are close to two billion Muslims, and most of them are not Arabs. The country with the most Muslims is Indonesia. After it come countries like Pakistan, India and Bangladesh. Nigeria, Egypt, Iran and Turkey each have tens of millions. Muslims speak hundreds of languages at home, from Javanese to Hausa to Bosnian to English. And yet five times a day, all of them turn to the same Arabic. A child in Jakarta and a grandmother in Dakar recite the Fatiha in the same sounds. The Qur'an names that variety as a sign. In Pickthall's words: "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours." Different tongues, one recitation. And each place has its own sound. Egypt gave the twentieth century many of its most famous reciters, whose long, melodic style filled radios around the world. In the Gulf, a plainer, flowing style is loved. Across North and West Africa, many recite in the reading of Warsh. Indonesia and Malaysia hold great national recitation competitions, where young men and women recite before huge crowds. Turkish reciters have their own ornamented tradition. Same words, different voices, and this week showed you why that holds together. The hafiz carries it by heart. The sajdah verses bring a room to the floor. The longest and the shortest, al-Baqarah and al-Kawthar. Who is speaking: We, I, He, and say. Handling the mushaf with care. Khatm, the whole book. And now the whole world, reciting it.
